text: In 1932, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight an army of birds.
The birds won.
I'm Sir Digsworth, and this is the Great Emu War.
It begins after the First World War. Australia gives thousands of its soldiers land in the west, to grow wheat.
Then comes the Great Depression. Wheat prices fall, and the help the government promised never arrives.
And then things get worse.
Twenty thousand emus arrive.
Every year, emus walk from the dry inland towards the coast. This year, they find something wonderful on the way: fields of wheat.
They eat the crops. They trample what they don't eat.
And they smash holes in the fences, which lets the rabbits in.
The farmers are old soldiers. So they ask for what soldiers know: machine guns.
The Minister of Defence says yes. After all, he says, the birds will make good target practice.
So the army sends one major, two soldiers, two machine guns and ten thousand bullets.
They even bring a film cameraman.
The second of November. The soldiers spot about fifty emus. But the birds stay just out of range.
The farmers try to herd them towards the guns. The emus split into small groups, and run.
Two days later, a better plan: an ambush, at a dam.
More than a thousand emus walk straight towards the gun. The soldiers wait, and wait, and open fire.
The gun jams.
Twelve birds down. A thousand gone.
The soldiers notice something odd. Every group of emus seems to have a leader: a big bird, six feet tall, with black feathers, who keeps watch and warns the others.
One bird expert wrote that the emu command had clearly ordered guerrilla tactics.
So the major tries speed. He puts a gun on a truck.
But the truck can't catch the birds, and the ride is so bumpy the gunner never fires a single shot.
After six days, the army has fired two and a half thousand bullets. Nobody is sure how many emus they hit. One count says fifty.
The major's report notes one comfort: his men suffered no casualties.
On the eighth of November, the army is called home.
The major is impressed. Emus, he says, can face machine guns like tanks.
In parliament, one politician asks whether the soldiers will get a medal.
But the emus are still eating. So five days later, the army comes back.
This time, it goes better. By December, they are shooting about a hundred emus a week.
Then the major is called home for good. His final score, by his own count: 986 emus, for 9,860 bullets.
That is exactly ten bullets for every bird.
The farmers ask for the army again in 1934, in 1943, and in 1948.
Each time, the government says no.
What finally works is much simpler: better fences, and a reward for every emu.
In six months of 1934, farmers claim more than fifty-seven thousand rewards.
And the emus?
They're still there.
Emus one. Australia nil.
I'm Sir Digsworth. Do mind the birds.
